analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal, federally funded child care and early learning program with fees capped at a sliding share of family income.
analysis.headline: The bill drew a Democratic sponsor and 96 Democratic cosponsors in the House, but was referred to committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made federal money available to states, cities, tribal organizations, and nonprofits to run child care and early learning programs open to every child too young for school, regardless of family income, disability, or citizenship status. Families below twice the poverty line would pay nothing, and no family would pay more than 7% of its income. It also set national program standards and required that child care staff be paid through a negotiated process with their unions.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children — especially low- and middle-income families now paying some of the highest child care costs in the world — would gain an entitlement to affordable care, with free care for families below 200% of the poverty line [S2][S3]. Child care workers would gain from required compensation standards and union bargaining rights [S3]. Parents would gain the ability to work or attend school without child care costs eating their paycheck.

how_it_helps.text: Every child not yet required to attend school would be entitled to a place in a program, regardless of family income, disability status, or citizenship status [S2][S3].
Families with incomes below 200% of the poverty line would pay no fees, and no family would pay more than 7% of its income regardless of income or number of children [S2][S3].

The federal government would cover at least 90% of program costs (100% for children of migrant and seasonal farmworkers and for Native American children), so localities would not bear most of the burden [S3].
Programs would run a full working day (at least 10 hours) and full calendar year, and providers would have to recognize and bargain with unions representing staff and home-based providers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an open-ended appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary') for a program where each covered child has an uncapped entitlement [S3]. With no revenue source or funding cap specified in the bill, the full multi-year cost would fall on the federal budget. Existing child care providers would also face fee caps and new wage and labor standards.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' and creates an uncapped entitlement — every covered child is entitled to a place — with no revenue source or spending limit specified, making its long-term cost very large and borne by federal taxpayers [S3].

Capping what families pay at 7% of income while paying providers would require a large public subsidy to keep providers operating; an honest supporter would acknowledge this is a permanent new federal spending commitment, not a one-time program [S2][S3].

Requiring union recognition, negotiated wages, and national program standards could raise costs for some existing providers and complicate participation, particularly for small home-based providers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to families is large and concrete: child care in the United States often costs more than college tuition, and this bill would cap what any family pays and make it free for the poorest. The cost is also real — an uncapped, open-ended federal entitlement of the kind estimated in the tens of billions per year for similar proposals — with no funding mechanism specified in the bill itself. The bill's design (building on Head Start and the military child care program rather than vouchers) is defensible, but its blank-check appropriations language is a genuine weakness an honest supporter would have to concede.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never held a markup or scheduled it for a floor vote, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Mikie Sherrill introduced the bill on February 9, 2023, with 34 original cosponsors [S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S5].
The bill accumulated 96 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].

The only action ever taken on the bill was the initial referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote was ever held, and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Families with young children lost the chance at affordable care and continue paying full child care costs. Existing child care providers keep their current pricing power and labor practices, and the federal budget avoided an open-ended new commitment.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: providers and current pricing

sides.party_line_note: All 96 cosponsors plus the sponsor were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would route large federal payments to providers as delegate providers of a new program, creating guaranteed demand [S3]. At the same time it caps what families pay, requires negotiated wages and union recognition, and imposes national program standards, ending the ability of providers to charge families whatever the market will bear [S3].

industries.industry: Child care and early learning workforce
industries.note: The bill requires compensation meeting federal standards and a collective process for staff and home-based providers to set wages, benefits, and working conditions — a direct pay raise mechanism for one of the lowest-paid workforces in the country [S3].
